positions.text: Fábrega and coauthors demonstrate that formal non-transferability does not by itself preserve one-person-one-account control. TEE-based key encumbrance can let one actor rent or direct voting rights across identity-verified wallets without transferring the underlying credential. The result supports the narrower proposition that Sybil resistance also requires control-binding assumptions or countermeasures; it does not show that every non-transferable identity design fails.
scope_conditions: wallet or credential control can be rented or delegated
the protected claim is treated as a negative sufficiency proposition

source_provenance.sourceProposition: Fábrega et al. show that identity systems intended to prevent Sybil accounts can remain insufficient when key encumbrance lets one actor control voting across identity-verified wallets.
source_provenance.exactEvidenceQuote: While whales splitting their tokens across Sybil accounts is a known attack on quadratic voting systems, identity systems alone (ensuring one user, one account to negate Sybils) are insufficient in the presence of key encumbrance.
